title: The one retention channel most businesses near 100k underuse
hook: The most valuable two weeks in a 100k business are the two weeks after the customer buys.
caption:
The most valuable two weeks in a 100k business are the two weeks after the customer buys.

Most owners treat this window like a formality. One welcome email goes out, and then the inbox goes quiet. The next message lands when there is a promotion, a product update, or a renewal coming up.

That is a missed window. A customer who just paid you is the most open to hearing from you they will ever be. The second purchase, the referral, the review, the habit, all of it starts here, and all of it fades week by week after.

Here are three things that fit inside those two weeks.

1. Send a short email on the day they buy, from a real person, that welcomes them and tells them what to expect over the next week. Keep it as a simple greeting, not a tutorial.

2. Check in again near day three or four. Ask one plain question. What are you trying to get done with this? You want a sentence back from them, not a survey.

3. Follow up in the second week and point them at the second thing your product or service can do for them. Frame it as a useful next step, not an upsell.

You do not need a clever sequence. You need to show up in the window that matters most.

title: How I rebuilt Passion.io's retention system: what I actually did
hook: How we lifted revenue per lead from $13 to $27 [verify with Muddassir] for a Passion.io client. Same list, same product, better use of what they already had.
tweets:
How we lifted revenue per lead from $13 to $27 [verify with Muddassir: final numbers, timeframe] for a Passion.io client in the online creator space.

No new traffic was added, and the list stayed the same size. The only thing that changed was how we wrote to the list they already had.

Here is a thread on what moved.

Where we started.

Standard broadcasts were going out to everyone on the list on the same day. Open rates looked fine on the surface. Revenue stayed flat all the same. The list was being shouted at, not written to.

First move. We split the list into three groups based on behaviour, not on list size.

Group A had bought in the last three months. Group B had bought six to eighteen months ago and had gone quiet. Group C had never bought but was still opening emails.

Group A is the easiest group to underpay attention to, because they already pay you.

We sent them an early access email twenty-four hours before anything went public. It read as a thank-you, not as a promotion. Revenue from this group doubled first.

Group B needed a specific reason to come back, not a "we miss you" line.

We wrote them about a new product that matched something they had bought before. It was a short message with a single link. That one message brought back a real slice of the group.

Group C needed the cleanest offer in the whole sequence. One clear hook, one clear saving, four emails across the window with rising urgency.

Accept that some of this group never buys, and write for the ones who will.

Send times mattered more than subject lines in the end.

Each group got a different send time that matched when their past opens had landed. There was no clever trick in it. We read what the data was already telling us.

Result. Revenue per lead almost doubled over the window [verify with Muddassir: exact figure].

Most of the lift came from Group A, which had the smallest send volume of the three. The list we had was already bigger than we were treating it.

Here is the move most businesses can copy this week.

Pull your list. Split it by last purchase date into three groups. Write one different email to each group. Send each group at a different time that matches their past opens. That is the whole project.

title: Why email is still the highest ROI channel for retention
hook: "Email is dead" is a line people use to avoid building the one channel they actually own.
caption:
"Email is dead" is a line people use to avoid building the one channel they actually own.

An inbox does not change its rules on you next week. It does not hold back a post because the first twenty likes were slow. It shows up the same way on a Tuesday as it does on a Sunday.

That is the channel most businesses near 100k are still not writing for.

title: LI Second Post: Welcome sequence fundamentals
hook: How to write the emails a new customer reads in the first week.
caption:
How to write the emails a new customer reads in the first week.

The first seven days after somebody buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them, and four emails across those days is usually enough.

Day 0. Keep it short and send it from a real person. Let them know what kind of business they have joined, and tell them what to expect from you over the next week.

Day 1. Point them at one small win they can get with the product or service today. You are not giving them a full tour, you are helping them finish one thing.

Day 3. Ask a single question. What are you trying to get done with this? One line back from them is worth more than any long survey.

Day 7. Suggest a standing time or a second use case. Something that turns a one-off purchase into a habit.

Four emails across one week. Rewrite yours if you have not looked at them in a year.

title: How to do cold outreach as a creative strategist and stand out
hook: Why cold outreach is still worth your time as a creative strategist, even in 2026.
caption:
Why cold outreach is still worth your time as a creative strategist, even in 2026.

Here is how I think about it. In my first year online I ran more than twenty million cold emails [verify with Muddassir: exact figure]. That is why I never needed to build a big audience first, and never starved for leads, and never slid into DMs for "networking."

Most people today will tell you cold outreach hurts your brand. My take on it runs the other way. If a creative strategist needs cold outreach at all, it usually means they do not have budget for anything else, and they have no leverage in the market yet, and no real brand built. A brand that does not exist cannot be hurt by outreach.

Done right, cold outreach is a volume game. If you cannot play volume, do not attempt it. If you can, it is the fastest way to prove to yourself that you can start and hold a conversation with a stranger. That skill does not go away.

Here is what cold outreach built for me. Hundreds of booked calls a month in that first year. Hundreds of tests on a single sentence. A rapport with strangers that let me ask for high-ticket work on the first call, because the first impression was never "please hire me." The first impression was "here is what I see in your business."

Here is what I would tell a creative strategist starting today. If you can run Facebook ads for yourself, that is probably a cleaner road to the same outcome. If you cannot, run cold outreach instead. Send messages that are not pitches at all. Send a piece of thinking about their business, with no rate, no ask, and no services page attached.

Ten messages sent properly will get you a handful of replies. A handful of replies will get you a paid conversation.

title: The outreach DM most creative strategists keep sending (and what to send instead)
hook: Your prospect reads that exact DM forty times a day.
caption:
Your prospect reads that exact DM forty times a day.

"Hey, I noticed your website could use some work" has been the opening line of outreach for the last five years. The prospect is numb to it, and they will skim past it before you finish the sentence.

Send a piece of thinking instead. Take a screenshot of one of their ads, and write three sentences on what you would test next. Do not attach a rate, do not attach an ask, and do not attach a services page. Just send the thinking.

title: Bad DM vs good DM, side by side
hook: Flattery is not personalization in cold outreach. Prospects can tell the difference in three seconds.
caption:
Flattery is not personalization in cold outreach, and prospects can tell the difference in three seconds.

One kind of message is flattery. "Love your content, love what you are doing." The other kind is observation. "Your Q4 ad is fading, and here is what I would test next."

If you are sending cold outreach as a creative strategist, send the second kind every time.
